title: Σκῆπτρον
about: Athena, sent by Hera and seen by Achilles alone, tells him to leave off the quarrel and keep his sword in its sheath, promising that three times as many gifts will one day be his; Achilles agrees that a word from the gods must be kept, and sheathes the sword. He then turns on Agamemnon again, calling him a drunkard with a dog’s eyes and a deer’s heart, and swears by the sceptre in his hand that the Achaeans will one day long for him and that Agamemnon will tear at his own heart in rage when Hector is killing them. He throws the sceptre down and sits. Nestor, the sweet-voiced old king of Pylos, rises and pleads with both men, telling of the great heroes he fought beside in his youth, and bidding Agamemnon not to take the girl and Achilles not to defy a king. Agamemnon agrees but will not be ruled, Achilles says he will not fight for the girl but will kill any man who tries to take anything else of his, and the assembly breaks up. Achilles goes to his huts and ships with Patroclus and his men, while Agamemnon launches a ship with twenty oarsmen, a hecatomb for Apollo and Chryseis, and sets Odysseus in command.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’: in Homer the article is a pronoun. The line is a formula, also found in the Odyssey, and the English is the same. αὖτε is ‘in turn, then’, and προσέειπε is the epic form of the aorist ‘addressed’. γλαυκῶπις, ‘gleaming-eyed’, is Athena’s stock epithet; it is built on γλαυκός ‘gleaming’, and what it means of an eye is disputed. Athena is the goddess Hera sent, as the poet said at 195.

sentences.t:
ἦλθον ἐγὼ παύσουσα τὸ σὸν μένος, αἴ κε πίθηαι,
οὐρανόθεν·
sentences.l:
“I came, I, to stop your fury, if you will obey,
from heaven;
sentences.i: “I came from the sky to stop your fury, if you will obey;
sentences.n: παύσουσα is a future participle of purpose, ‘to stop’, feminine because Athena speaks of herself, and ἐγώ stresses ‘I’. αἴ κε πίθηαι is ‘if you will obey’: αἰ = εἰ, κε = ἄν, and πίθηαι is the epic aorist subjunctive of πείθομαι. μένος is the surge of anger that rises in a man, ‘fury’ as at 103. οὐρανόθεν has the suffix -θεν, ‘from’, so ‘from heaven’. The edition prints a stop after it.

sentences.t:
πρὸ δέ μ’ ἧκε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη
ἄμφω ὁμῶς θυμῷ φιλέουσά τε κηδομένη τε·
sentences.l:
and forth me sent the goddess, white-armed Hera,
both alike in heart loving and caring for;
sentences.i: and the goddess, white-armed Hera, sent me forth, loving and caring for both alike in her heart;
sentences.n: πρὸ … ἧκε is a tmesis, the preverb standing apart: προῆκε ‘sent forth’, and μ’ is με ‘me’. The second line is word for word 196, where the poet said it of Hera; now Athena says it. ἄμφω ‘both’ is not named; the two are Achilles and Agamemnon. φιλέουσα and κηδομένη are participles agreeing with Hera: ‘loving’ and ‘caring for’. λευκώλενος is ‘white-armed’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε λῆγ’ ἔριδος, μηδὲ ξίφος ἕλκεο χειρί·
sentences.l: But come, give up strife, and do not draw the sword with your hand;
sentences.i: But come, give up this strife, and do not draw the sword with your hand;
sentences.n: Two commands follow ἀλλ’ ἄγε ‘but come’. λῆγε is the imperative of λήγω ‘cease from’, with the genitive ἔριδος ‘strife’. μηδὲ … ἕλκεο forbids with the present imperative middle of ἕλκω ‘draw’: ‘do not go on drawing’, since he has already begun to draw the sword. ξίφος is ‘sword’, and χειρί ‘with your hand’ is a dative of instrument.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι ἔπεσιν μὲν ὀνείδισον ὡς ἔσεταί περ·
sentences.l: But indeed with words reproach him, just as it will be;
sentences.i: But reproach him with words, just as it shall be;
sentences.n: ἤτοι is printed as one word, ‘indeed’. ἔπεσιν is the dative plural of ἔπος, ‘with words’, set against the sword, and ὀνείδισον is the aorist imperative of ὀνειδίζω ‘reproach’. The last clause, ὡς ἔσεταί περ, ‘just as it will be’, is obscure; it is usually taken to mean ‘however it turns out’, and the translation keeps it as close to the Greek as English allows. The Greek gives no object for ὀνείδισον; ‘him’, Agamemnon, is supplied. ἔσεται is the epic future of εἰμί.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἐξερέω, τὸ δὲ καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.l: For thus I will declare, and this too fulfilled shall be;
sentences.i: For I will say it in this way, and what I say will also be fulfilled:
sentences.n: The line is word for word one in the Odyssey, and the English is the same. ὧδε is ‘in this way’; ἐξερέω is ‘I will say out’, ἐκ with the future of εἶπον. τετελεσμένον is the perfect passive participle of τελέω, ‘fulfilled’, and ἔσται ‘will be’. What follows, the promise of gifts, is what Athena says will be fulfilled.

sentences.t:
καί ποτέ τοι τρὶς τόσσα παρέσσεται ἀγλαὰ δῶρα
ὕβριος εἵνεκα τῆσδε·
sentences.l:
And some day, for you, three times so many will be at hand, splendid gifts,
on account of this insolence;
sentences.i: And some day three times as many splendid gifts will be yours, on account of this insolence;
sentences.n: καί ποτέ is ‘and some day’. τρὶς τόσσα is ‘three times as many’, the subject of παρέσσεται, the epic future of πάρειμι, ‘will be at hand’, with τοι = σοι ‘for you’. ἀγλαὰ δῶρα are ‘splendid gifts’. ὕβριος εἵνεκα τῆσδε is ‘on account of this insolence’: εἵνεκα = ἕνεκα follows its noun, and ὕβρις is violent, contemptuous behaviour, as at 203. The insolence is Agamemnon’s.

sentences.t: σὺ δ’ ἴσχεο, πείθεο δ’ ἡμῖν.
sentences.l: but you, hold yourself back, and obey us.”
sentences.i: but hold yourself back, and obey us.”
sentences.n: ἴσχεο is the present imperative middle of ἴσχω, ‘hold yourself back’, and πείθεο is the uncontracted imperative of πείθομαι ‘obey’, with the dative ἡμῖν ‘us’: Athena and Hera. The speech ends on the double command.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to her:
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘her’ (the article as a pronoun), the object of προσέφη ‘addressed’, and ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’. This is the reply-formula, feminine here because the listener is a goddess. πόδας ὠκύς, ‘swift in feet’, is Achilles’ stock epithet: πόδας is an accusative of respect, ‘in respect of his feet’.

sentences.t:
χρὴ μὲν σφωΐτερόν γε θεὰ ἔπος εἰρύσσασθαι
καὶ μάλα περ θυμῷ κεχολωμένον·
sentences.l:
“Needful it is, goddess, the word of you two to keep,
even though greatly in heart angered;
sentences.i: “Goddess, one must keep the word of you two, even when very angry at heart;
sentences.n: χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes the infinitive εἰρύσσασθαι, ‘to keep’, and the object is σφωΐτερον ἔπος ‘the word of you two’: σφωΐτερος is the dual possessive, ‘belonging to the two of you’, Athena and Hera. The unstated subject is Achilles himself, so κεχολωμένον, the perfect passive participle of χολόω ‘anger’, is accusative: ‘even though one is greatly angered in heart’. θεά is a vocative.

sentences.t: ὧς γὰρ ἄμεινον·
sentences.l: for thus it is better;
sentences.i: for it is better so;
sentences.n: ὧς is the old adverb ‘thus, so’, and ἄμεινον ‘better’ is the comparative of ἀγαθός, with ἐστί understood. The clause gives the reason for the whole sentence before it: obedience is the better course.

sentences.t: ὅς κε θεοῖς ἐπιπείθηται μάλα τ’ ἔκλυον αὐτοῦ.
sentences.l: whoever obeys the gods, greatly they hear him.”
sentences.i: whoever obeys the gods, they hear him well.”
sentences.n: ὅς κε with the subjunctive ἐπιπείθηται (ἐπιπείθομαι ‘obey’) makes a general statement, ‘whoever obeys the gods’. μάλα τ’ ἔκλυον αὐτοῦ is ‘they hear him greatly’: ἔκλυον is the aorist of κλύω ‘hear’, used for what always happens, and takes the genitive αὐτοῦ; τε is the epic τε of a general truth. The subject, understood, is the gods.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ ἐπ’ ἀργυρέῃ κώπῃ σχέθε χεῖρα βαρεῖαν,
ἂψ δ’ ἐς κουλεὸν ὦσε μέγα ξίφος, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε
μύθῳ Ἀθηναίης·
sentences.i: So he said, and held his heavy hand on the hilt of silver, and thrust the great sword back into its sheath, and did not disobey the word of Athena;
sentences.n: ἦ καί is ‘he spoke, and’: ἦ is the old ‘he said’, and the phrase closes the speech and starts the action. σχέθε is the aorist of ἔχω, ‘held’, and ἐπὶ … κώπῃ is ‘on the hilt’, which is of silver (ἀργυρέῃ). κουλεόν is the Ionic κολεόν ‘sheath’, ὦσε the aorist of ὠθέω ‘thrust’, and οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ‘nor disobeyed’ takes the dative μύθῳ ‘word’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ Οὔλυμπον δὲ βεβήκει
δώματ’ ἐς αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς μετὰ δαίμονας ἄλλους.
sentences.l:
and she to Olympus had gone,
to the halls of aegis-bearing Zeus, among the other divinities.
sentences.i: but she had gone to Olympus, to the halls of aegis-bearing Zeus, among the other divinities.
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ is ‘but she’, Athena. The -δε of Οὔλυμπον δέ is the suffix of direction, ‘to Olympus’, and βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had gone’. αἰγιόχοιο, ‘aegis-bearing’, is a stock epithet of Zeus whose meaning is disputed. δαίμονας is ‘divinities’, the word for a god seen as a power; here it simply means the other gods.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης δ’ ἐξαῦτις ἀταρτηροῖς ἐπέεσσιν
Ἀτρεΐδην προσέειπε, καὶ οὔ πω λῆγε χόλοιο·
sentences.l:
And Peleus’-son again with harsh words
Atreus’-son addressed, and not yet ceased from anger:
sentences.i: And the son of Peleus again addressed the son of Atreus with harsh words, and he had not yet ceased from his anger:
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης and Ἀτρεΐδην are patronymics, ‘son of Peleus’ and ‘son of Atreus’: Achilles and Agamemnon. ἐξαῦτις is ‘again’, and ἐπέεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ἔπος. ἀταρτηροῖς is a rare adjective, explained in antiquity as ‘harmful, mischievous’; its origin is not known, and ‘harsh’ is a guess in that direction. λῆγε is the imperfect of λήγω, the verb of the command at 210, with the genitive χόλοιο ‘anger’.

sentences.t:
οἰνοβαρές, κυνὸς ὄμματ’ ἔχων, κραδίην δ’ ἐλάφοιο,
οὔτέ ποτ’ ἐς πόλεμον ἅμα λαῷ θωρηχθῆναι
οὔτε λόχον δ’ ἰέναι σὺν ἀριστήεσσιν Ἀχαιῶν
τέτληκας θυμῷ·
sentences.l:
“Heavy with wine, with a dog’s eyes in you, and a deer’s heart,
neither ever for war with the people to arm yourself
nor to an ambush to go with the best of the Achaeans
have you dared in heart;
sentences.i: “You who are weighed down with wine, with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer, you have never dared in your heart to arm for war together with the people, or to go into an ambush with the best of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: A run of insults, opening with the vocative οἰνοβαρές ‘heavy with wine’ (οἶνος + βάρος). The dog is the shameless animal, as in κυνῶπα at 159, and the deer the timid one; κραδίη (= καρδία) and θυμός both mean ‘heart’. The infinitives θωρηχθῆναι (aorist passive of θωρήσσω ‘arm’) and ἰέναι depend on τέτληκας, perfect of τλάω, here ‘have dared’. λόχον is an ambush, and ἀριστήεσσιν the epic dative plural of ἀριστεύς ‘best man’.

sentences.t: τὸ δέ τοι κὴρ εἴδεται εἶναι.
sentences.l: and that to you seems to be a death-spirit.
sentences.i: but to you that looks like a spirit of death.
sentences.n: τὸ is ‘that’: arming for war and going to an ambush. τοι = σοι ‘to you’, and εἴδεται εἶναι is ‘seems to be’. κήρ is a death-spirit, a power that carries a man off to death; the nominative κὴρ is not the other word κῆρ ‘heart’. Achilles says Agamemnon sees death in the very things that make a warrior.

sentences.t:
ἦ πολὺ λώϊόν ἐστι κατὰ στρατὸν εὐρὺν Ἀχαιῶν
δῶρ’ ἀποαιρεῖσθαι ὅς τις σέθεν ἀντίον εἴπῃ·
sentences.l:
Truly it is much better, throughout the wide host of the Achaeans,
to take away the gifts of whoever speaks against you;
sentences.i: Truly it is far better, throughout the wide host of the Achaeans, to take away the gifts of anyone who speaks against you;
sentences.n: ἦ is ‘truly’. λώϊον, ‘better’, is a comparative of ἀγαθός, with ἐστί, and the infinitive ἀποαιρεῖσθαι ‘to take away’ is the subject. κατὰ στρατὸν εὐρύν is ‘throughout the wide host’. δῶρα ‘gifts’ means what the army has given a man, such as prizes. σέθεν is the epic genitive of σύ, governed by ἀντίον ‘against’, and ὅς τις … εἴπῃ is a general ‘whoever speaks’.

sentences.t: δημοβόρος βασιλεὺς ἐπεὶ οὐτιδανοῖσιν ἀνάσσεις·
sentences.l: a people-devouring king, since over worthless men you are lord;
sentences.i: you king who devour your people, since you are lord over worthless men;
sentences.n: δημοβόρος ‘people-devouring’ is δῆμος ‘people’ with the root of βορά ‘food’: a king who feeds on his people. It is a nominative in apposition to the ‘you’ inside ἀνάσσεις. ἐπεί ‘since’ gives the reason he can: he is lord over οὐτιδανοῖσιν, ‘worthless men’, dative after ἀνάσσω ‘be lord over’, men of no account who will not resist.

sentences.t: ἦ γὰρ ἂν Ἀτρεΐδη νῦν ὕστατα λωβήσαιο.
sentences.l: for truly, Atreus’-son, now for the last time you would do outrage.
sentences.i: For truly, son of Atreus, this would now be the last outrage you committed.
sentences.n: ἦ γὰρ ἂν … λωβήσαιο has ἄν with the aorist optative of λωβάομαι, ‘treat outrageously’: a potential, ‘you would be doing outrage’. ὕστατα ‘for the last time’ is the neuter plural of ὕστατος used as an adverb. Ἀτρεΐδη is a vocative. The thought is that Agamemnon gets away with his insults only because no one stands up to him; otherwise this would be his last.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔκ τοι ἐρέω καὶ ἐπὶ μέγαν ὅρκον ὀμοῦμαι·
sentences.l: But I will speak out plainly to you, and upon it a great oath I will swear:
sentences.i: But I will tell you plainly, and I will swear a great oath on it:
sentences.n: ἔκ τοι ἐρέω is a tmesis for ἐξερέω ‘I will speak out’ (as at 204), with τοι = σοι. ἐπὶ … ὀμοῦμαι is another, ἐπομοῦμαι ‘I will swear upon it’, the future of ὄμνυμι. μέγαν ὅρκον ‘a great oath’ is the oath that follows, sworn on the sceptre.

sentences.t:
ναὶ μὰ τόδε σκῆπτρον, τὸ μὲν οὔ ποτε φύλλα καὶ ὄζους
φύσει, ἐπεὶ δὴ πρῶτα τομὴν ἐν ὄρεσσι λέλοιπεν,
οὐδ’ ἀναθηλήσει·
sentences.i: Yes, by this sceptre, which will never put forth leaves or branches, since it first left its stump behind in the mountains, and will not flourish again;
sentences.n: ναὶ μά ‘yes, by’ takes the accusative τόδε σκῆπτρον ‘this sceptre’, which Achilles holds. The relative clause says it is dead wood: οὔ ποτε … φύσει ‘will never put forth’ (future of φύω) φύλλα καὶ ὄζους ‘leaves and branches’; λέλοιπεν, perfect of λείπω, with τομήν ‘the stump, the cut’, ‘left its stump’ on ὄρεσσι, the epic dative plural of ὄρος ‘mountain’. οὐδ’ ἀναθηλήσει is ‘nor will it flourish again’, from ἀναθάλλω.

sentences.t:
περὶ γάρ ῥά ἑ χαλκὸς ἔλεψε
φύλλά τε καὶ φλοιόν·
sentences.l:
for all around it the bronze stripped
leaves and bark;
sentences.i: for the bronze stripped it all round, leaves and bark alike;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason the sceptre will never grow again. περί is an adverb, ‘all round’, with ἔλεψε, the aorist of λέπω ‘peel, strip’. ἑ is the pronoun ‘it’, ῥά = ἄρα, and φύλλά τε καὶ φλοιόν, ‘leaves and bark’, are the things stripped, a second accusative. χαλκός is bronze, the blade that cut and stripped the branch.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖτέ μιν υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
ἐν παλάμῃς φορέουσι δικασπόλοι, οἵ τε θέμιστας
πρὸς Διὸς εἰρύαται·
sentences.i: and now in their turn the sons of the Achaeans, who dispense justice, carry it in their palms, and keep the rules of right that come from Zeus;
sentences.n: νῦν αὖτε is ‘now in turn’, and μιν is ‘it’, the sceptre. δικασπόλοι is ‘justice-tending’, in apposition to υἷες Ἀχαιῶν ‘the sons of the Achaeans’: the men who give judgments. ἐν παλάμῃς is the epic dative plural, ‘in their palms’. θέμιστες are rules of right, and εἰρύαται is the perfect of εἰρύομαι ‘guard, keep’, third plural; πρὸς Διός means ‘from Zeus’, as his rulings, under his protection.

sentences.t: ὃ δέ τοι μέγας ἔσσεται ὅρκος·
sentences.l: and this shall be for you a great oath;
sentences.i: and this will be a great oath for you;
sentences.n: ὃ is the pronoun ‘this’, the sceptre and what is sworn by it, and τοι = σοι ‘for you’. ἔσσεται is the epic future of εἰμί. μέγας ὅρκος picks up μέγαν ὅρκον of 233: the oath itself follows in the next lines.

sentences.t:
ἦ ποτ’ Ἀχιλλῆος ποθὴ ἵξεται υἷας Ἀχαιῶν
σύμπαντας·
sentences.l:
Truly some day a lack of Achilles will come upon the sons of the Achaeans,
all of them;
sentences.i: Truly some day the lack of Achilles will come upon the sons of the Achaeans, all of them;
sentences.n: ἦ ποτε is ‘truly some day’. ποθή is a longing or want for one who is absent, from the root of πόθος; ‘lack’ keeps the idea that his absence will be felt as a want. It is the subject of ἵξεται, the future of ἵκω ‘come to’, with the accusative υἷας Ἀχαιῶν σύμπαντας, ‘all the sons of the Achaeans’. Ἀχιλλῆος is the genitive, ‘of Achilles’.

sentences.t:
τότε δ’ οὔ τι δυνήσεαι ἀχνύμενός περ
χραισμεῖν, εὖτ’ ἂν πολλοὶ ὑφ’ Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο
θνήσκοντες πίπτωσι·
sentences.i: and then, grieving as you may, you will be unable to help when many fall dying at the hands of man-slaying Hector;
sentences.n: δυνήσεαι is the uncontracted future of δύναμαι, ‘you will be able’, and ἀχνύμενός περ ‘grieving though you are’ makes the participle concessive. χραισμεῖν is ‘to avail, help’. εὖτ’ ἂν … πίπτωσι is ‘when … fall’, a general subjunctive. ὑφ’ Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο is ‘by man-slaying Hector’: ὑπό with the genitive of the agent, and ἀνδροφόνος ‘man-slaying’ (ἀνήρ + the root of φόνος) is the epithet of Hector, a Trojan.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ ἔνδοθι θυμὸν ἀμύξεις
χωόμενος ὅ τ’ ἄριστον Ἀχαιῶν οὐδὲν ἔτισας.
sentences.l:
and you within will tear your heart,
incensed that the best of the Achaeans you honoured not at all.”
sentences.i: and you will tear at your own heart within, incensed that you paid no honour at all to the best of the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: ἔνδοθι is ‘within’, and ἀμύξεις is the future of ἀμύσσω ‘tear, scratch’, here the heart torn by remorse. χωόμενος is ‘incensed’, the participle of χώομαι. ὅ τ’ is ὅ τε ‘because’, and οὐδὲν ἔτισας is ‘you honoured in nothing’: ἔτισας is the aorist of τίω ‘honour’. ἄριστον Ἀχαιῶν, ‘the best of the Achaeans’, is Achilles himself. The speech ends.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο Πηλεΐδης, ποτὶ δὲ σκῆπτρον βάλε γαίῃ
χρυσείοις ἥλοισι πεπαρμένον, ἕζετο δ’ αὐτός·
sentences.l:
So spoke Peleus’-son, and down the sceptre he dashed to the ground
pierced with golden studs, and sat down himself;
sentences.i: So spoke the son of Peleus, and dashed the sceptre to the ground, with its golden studs set in it, and sat down himself;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’, and ποτὶ … βάλε is a tmesis, ‘dashed down’ (the Odyssey has the same clause of Telemachus), with βάλε unaugmented and γαίῃ the dative ‘to the ground’. πεπαρμένον is the perfect passive participle of πείρω ‘pierce’, agreeing with σκῆπτρον: the staff is studded with χρυσείοις ἥλοισι, ‘golden studs’ (ἧλος is a nail or stud). ἕζετο is ‘sat down’ and αὐτός ‘himself’.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐμήνιε·
sentences.l: And Atreus’-son on the other side was wrathful;
sentences.i: while the son of Atreus on his side was wrathful;
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδης is Agamemnon, and ἑτέρωθεν, with the suffix -θεν, is ‘from the other side’. ἐμήνιε is the imperfect of μηνίω ‘be wrathful’, from μῆνις ‘wrath’, the poem’s first word, now used of a king’s anger. The line goes on into Nestor’s entrance, which opens the next unit.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ Νέστωρ
ἡδυεπὴς ἀνόρουσε λιγὺς Πυλίων ἀγορητής,
τοῦ καὶ ἀπὸ γλώσσης μέλιτος γλυκίων ῥέεν αὐδή·
sentences.i: and among them Nestor sprang up, sweet of speech, the clear-voiced speaker of the Pylians, from whose tongue the voice flowed sweeter than honey;
sentences.n: Nestor enters with his epithets: ἡδυεπής ‘sweet of speech’ (ἡδύς + ἔπος), λιγύς ‘clear-voiced’, and Πυλίων ἀγορητής ‘speaker of the Pylians’ (Πυλίων is the genitive plural). ἀνόρουσε is the aorist ‘sprang up’. τοῦ is the relative ‘whose’; μέλιτος γλυκίων is ‘sweeter than honey’, γλυκίων the comparative of γλυκύς with the genitive of comparison. ῥέεν is ‘flowed’ and αὐδή ‘voice, speech’.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἤδη δύο μὲν γενεαὶ μερόπων ἀνθρώπων
ἐφθίαθ’, οἵ οἱ πρόσθεν ἅμα τράφεν ἠδ’ ἐγένοντο
ἐν Πύλῳ ἠγαθέῃ, μετὰ δὲ τριτάτοισιν ἄνασσεν·
sentences.i: In his lifetime two generations of men of articulate speech had already perished, who had been reared and born with him in holy Pylos in earlier days, and now he was lord among the third;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘for him’, ‘in his lifetime’. The meaning of μερόπων in μερόπων ἀνθρώπων is not known; the ancient explanation, ‘with divided speech’, i.e. articulate, is followed here. ἐφθίαθ’ is ἐφθίατο, the pluperfect of φθίω ‘perish’; οἵ is ‘who’ and οἱ ‘with him’; τράφεν is the epic aorist passive of τρέφω ‘were reared’. Πύλῳ ἠγαθέῃ is ‘holy Pylos’, and ἄνασσεν the unaugmented imperfect of ἀνάσσω ‘be lord’.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐὺ φρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: This line is word for word 73, where Calchas rose to speak, and the English is the same. ὅ is ‘he’ (the article as a pronoun), σφιν ‘to them’, and ἐὺ φρονέων ‘thinking well’, i.e. kindly disposed toward them. ἀγορήσατο is the aorist of ἀγοράομαι, ‘addressed the assembly’, and μετέειπεν ‘spoke among’ them.

sentences.t: ὦ πόποι ἦ μέγα πένθος Ἀχαιΐδα γαῖαν ἱκάνει·
sentences.l: “Ah! truly a great grief comes upon the Achaean country;
sentences.i: “Ah, truly a great grief comes upon the Achaean country;
sentences.n: ὦ πόποι is a cry of dismay, ‘Ah!’, and ἦ is ‘truly’. μέγα πένθος ‘a great grief’ is the subject of ἱκάνει ‘comes upon, reaches’, and Ἀχαιΐδα γαῖαν ‘the Achaean country’ (Ἀχαιΐς is the feminine of ‘Achaean’) its object. Nestor opens by naming the harm to the whole army, not to either king.

sentences.t:
ἦ κεν γηθήσαι Πρίαμος Πριάμοιό τε παῖδες
ἄλλοι τε Τρῶες μέγα κεν κεχαροίατο θυμῷ
εἰ σφῶϊν τάδε πάντα πυθοίατο μαρναμένοιϊν,
οἳ περὶ μὲν βουλὴν Δαναῶν, περὶ δ’ ἐστὲ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
Truly Priam would rejoice, and Priam’s sons,
and the other Trojans greatly would be glad in heart,
if of you two all this they were to hear, as you contend,
you who surpass the Danaans in counsel, and surpass them in fighting.
sentences.i: Truly Priam would rejoice, and the sons of Priam, and the other Trojans would be greatly glad in heart, if they were to hear all this about the two of you contending, you who surpass the Danaans in counsel and surpass them in fighting.
sentences.n: Four lines, one sentence. ἦ κεν γηθήσαι … κεν κεχαροίατο are potential optatives (‘would rejoice … would be glad’, of γηθέω and χαίρω), and εἰ … πυθοίατο is the condition, ‘if they were to learn’ (aorist optative of πυνθάνομαι). σφῶϊν μαρναμένοιϊν is a dual, ‘of you two contending’. οἳ περὶ μὲν βουλήν … περὶ δ’ ἐστὲ μάχεσθαι: περί means ‘beyond’, with ἐστέ ‘you surpass’, and Δαναῶν is the genitive of comparison.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ πίθεσθ’·
sentences.l: But obey;
sentences.i: But obey me;
sentences.n: πίθεσθ’ is πίθεσθε, the aorist imperative middle of πείθομαι ‘obey’, in the plural although two men are addressed; the next unit uses the dual. The edition prints a stop after it, and the command is then given its reason.

sentences.t: ἄμφω δὲ νεωτέρω ἐστὸν ἐμεῖο·
sentences.l: both of you are younger than I;
sentences.i: you are both younger than I am;
sentences.n: ἄμφω … νεωτέρω ἐστόν is dual throughout: ἄμφω ‘both’, νεωτέρω ‘younger’ (comparative of νέος) and ἐστόν ‘you two are’. ἐμεῖο is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, the genitive of comparison: ‘than I’.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γάρ ποτ’ ἐγὼ καὶ ἀρείοσιν ἠέ περ ὑμῖν
ἀνδράσιν ὡμίλησα, καὶ οὔ ποτέ μ’ οἵ γ’ ἀθέριζον.
sentences.l:
For already once I with better, than even you,
men kept company, and never did they slight me.
sentences.i: For once before I kept company with men even better than you, and they never slighted me.
sentences.n: ἤδη … ποτέ is ‘once before’. ἀρείοσιν, ‘better’, is the dative plural of ἀρείων, a comparative of ἀγαθός, agreeing with ἀνδράσιν; ἠέ περ ὑμῖν is ‘than even you’, with ἠέ = ἤ ‘than’. ὡμίλησα is ‘I kept company with’ (ὁμιλέω) with the dative. ἀθέριζον is the imperfect of ἀθερίζω ‘slight, make light of’, with οἵ γ’ ‘they’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πω τοίους ἴδον ἀνέρας οὐδὲ ἴδωμαι,
οἷον Πειρίθοόν τε Δρύαντά τε ποιμένα λαῶν
Καινέα τ’ Ἐξάδιόν τε καὶ ἀντίθεον Πολύφημον
Θησέα τ’ Αἰγεΐδην, ἐπιείκελον ἀθανάτοισιν·
sentences.l:
For never yet such men have I seen, nor shall I see,
as Peirithous, and Dryas, shepherd of the people,
and Caeneus, and Exadius, and godlike Polyphemus,
and Theseus, son of Aegeus, resembling the immortals;
sentences.i: For never yet have I seen such men, nor shall I ever see them, as Peirithous and Dryas, shepherd of the people, and Caeneus and Exadius and godlike Polyphemus, and Theseus, son of Aegeus, like the immortals;
sentences.n: A list of the heroes of Nestor’s youth. οὐ γάρ πω … ἴδον is ‘for never yet have I seen’ (ἴδον is unaugmented), οὐδὲ ἴδωμαι ‘nor shall I’ (aorist subjunctive), and οἷον ‘such as’ introduces the names, ἀνέρας being the epic form of ἄνδρας. ποιμένα λαῶν is ‘shepherd of the people’, a title for a leader; this Polyphemus is a hero, not the Cyclops of the Odyssey. Αἰγεΐδην is ‘son of Aegeus’, and ἐπιείκελον ἀθανάτοισιν ‘resembling the immortals’.

sentences.t: κάρτιστοι δὴ κεῖνοι ἐπιχθονίων τράφεν ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l: Strongest indeed were those, of men on earth reared;
sentences.i: Those were the strongest of the men reared on the earth;
sentences.n: κάρτιστοι, ‘strongest’, is an epic superlative from κάρτος ‘strength’, related to κρατερός. κεῖνοι is ἐκεῖνοι ‘those’, and τράφεν ‘were reared’ is the same form as at 251. ἐπιχθονίων ἀνδρῶν, ‘men upon the earth’, is a genitive of the group they are the best of: mortal men.

sentences.t:
κάρτιστοι μὲν ἔσαν καὶ καρτίστοις ἐμάχοντο
φηρσὶν ὀρεσκῴοισι καὶ ἐκπάγλως ἀπόλεσσαν.
sentences.l:
strongest they were, and with the strongest they fought,
the mountain-bedded beasts, and terribly destroyed them.
sentences.i: They were the strongest, and they fought against the strongest, the beasts of the mountains, and destroyed them terribly.
sentences.n: κάρτιστοι … καρτίστοις is the same word twice, ‘strongest … against the strongest’, the second a dative after ἐμάχοντο ‘fought’; ἔσαν is ἦσαν. φήρ is the Aeolic form of θήρ ‘wild beast’, and ὀρεσκῷος is traditionally explained as ‘lying on the mountains’; the Greek does not name the beasts, and ancient readers took them to be the Centaurs. ἐκπάγλως is the adverb of ἔκπαγλος ‘terrifying’, and ἀπόλεσσαν the aorist of ἀπόλλυμι with epic doubled σ.

sentences.t:
καὶ μὲν τοῖσιν ἐγὼ μεθομίλεον ἐκ Πύλου ἐλθὼν
τηλόθεν ἐξ ἀπίης γαίης·
sentences.l:
And with them indeed I kept company, from Pylos having come
from far away, from a distant land;
sentences.i: And I joined their company too, having come from Pylos, from far away, from a distant land;
sentences.n: καὶ μέν is ‘and indeed’. μεθομίλεον is the imperfect of μεθομιλέω ‘join the company of’, with the dative τοῖσιν ‘them’. ἐκ Πύλου ἐλθών is ‘having come from Pylos’ and τηλόθεν ‘from afar’. ἀπίη in ἐξ ἀπίης γαίης is a rare adjective, explained in antiquity as ‘far-off’; ‘a distant land’ follows that explanation, though it is not certain.

sentences.t: καλέσαντο γὰρ αὐτοί·
sentences.l: for they themselves summoned me;
sentences.i: for they themselves summoned me;
sentences.n: καλέσαντο is the aorist middle of καλέω, ‘they summoned’, the middle suggesting ‘to themselves’, and the object ‘me’ is not expressed. αὐτοί ‘themselves’ says the call came from them. γάρ gives the reason Nestor, who came from far away, joined them.

sentences.t: καὶ μαχόμην κατ’ ἔμ’ αὐτὸν ἐγώ·
sentences.l: and I fought on my own account, I myself;
sentences.i: and I fought on my own;
sentences.n: μαχόμην is the imperfect middle of μάχομαι ‘fight’. κατ’ ἔμ’ αὐτὸν ἐγώ, ‘by myself’, is κατά with the accusative, ‘on my own account’, and ἐγώ is emphatic. Nestor claims to have fought as a man in his own right among those great men.

sentences.t:
κείνοισι δ’ ἂν οὔ τις
τῶν οἳ νῦν βροτοί εἰσιν ἐπιχθόνιοι μαχέοιτο·
sentences.l:
and with those none
of those who now are mortals on earth would fight;
sentences.i: and none of the mortals who live on earth now could fight against them;
sentences.n: κείνοισι is ἐκείνοισι ‘with those’, a dative after μαχέοιτο, the uncontracted optative of μάχομαι with ἂν, a potential: ‘none would fight’, i.e. none could. τῶν οἳ νῦν βροτοί εἰσιν ἐπιχθόνιοι is ‘of those who are now mortals upon the earth’, the same ἐπιχθόνιος as in 266.

sentences.t: καὶ μέν μευ βουλέων ξύνιεν πείθοντό τε μύθῳ·
sentences.l: And indeed my counsels they understood, and obeyed my word;
sentences.i: And they took in my counsels and obeyed my word;
sentences.n: μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, ‘my’. ξύνιεν is the imperfect of συνίημι ‘take in, understand’ (third plural), with the genitive βουλέων, the uncontracted genitive plural of βουλή ‘counsel’. πείθοντο τε μύθῳ is ‘and they obeyed my word’, the imperfect middle of πείθομαι with the dative.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ πίθεσθε καὶ ὔμμες, ἐπεὶ πείθεσθαι ἄμεινον·
sentences.l: But obey, you too, since to obey is better;
sentences.i: So you too must obey, since obeying is better;
sentences.n: ὔμμες is the Aeolic form of ὑμεῖς ‘you’, with καί ‘also’. ἐπεὶ πείθεσθαι ἄμεινον is ‘since to obey is better’: the infinitive is the subject and ἐστί is understood. This is the thought Achilles gave Athena at 217, now turned on Achilles himself and Agamemnon.

sentences.t:
μήτε σὺ τόνδ’ ἀγαθός περ ἐὼν ἀποαίρεο κούρην,
ἀλλ’ ἔα ὥς οἱ πρῶτα δόσαν γέρας υἷες Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l:
Nor you, good though you are, take from this man the maiden,
but allow it, as to him at first they gave the prize, the sons of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: And do not you, good as you are, take the maiden from this man, but let it stand as the sons of the Achaeans first gave her to him as his prize of honour;
sentences.n: Nestor now speaks to Agamemnon: μήτε … μήτε ‘neither … nor’ governs two commands. ἀποαίρεο is the present imperative middle of ἀφαιρέομαι ‘take away’, with τόνδε ‘this man’ (Achilles, standing there) and κούρην ‘maiden’ as its two objects. ἀγαθός περ ἐών is ‘good though you are’. ἔα is the imperative of ἐάω ‘allow’; οἱ is ‘to him’, and δόσαν is the unaugmented aorist ‘they gave’. γέρας is the prize.

sentences.t:
μήτε σὺ Πηλείδη ἔθελ’ ἐριζέμεναι βασιλῆϊ
ἀντιβίην, ἐπεὶ οὔ ποθ’ ὁμοίης ἔμμορε τιμῆς
σκηπτοῦχος βασιλεύς, ᾧ τε Ζεὺς κῦδος ἔδωκεν.
sentences.l:
nor you, son of Peleus, be willing to strive with a king
in opposition, since never of equal honour has a share
a sceptre-holding king, to whom Zeus has given glory.
sentences.i: and do not you, son of Peleus, choose to strive against a king in open opposition, since a sceptred king, to whom Zeus has given glory, never has an equal share of honour.
sentences.n: Now Nestor turns to Achilles: Πηλείδη is the vocative of the patronymic. ἔθελ’ is the present imperative of ἐθέλω, so ‘do not be willing’, with the infinitive ἐριζέμεναι ‘to strive’ and the dative βασιλῆϊ ‘with a king’; ἀντιβίην is an adverbial accusative, ‘in open opposition’. ἔμμορε, the perfect of μείρομαι, takes the genitive: ‘has a share of’ ὁμοίης τιμῆς ‘equal honour’. σκηπτοῦχος βασιλεύς is ‘a sceptre-holding king’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ σὺ καρτερός ἐσσι θεὰ δέ σε γείνατο μήτηρ,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε φέρτερός ἐστιν ἐπεὶ πλεόνεσσιν ἀνάσσει.
sentences.l:
But if you are strong, and a goddess mother bore you,
yet he is stronger, since he is lord over more.
sentences.i: Even if you are strong, and a goddess was your mother, he is still the stronger, because he is lord over more men.
sentences.n: εἰ δέ … ἀλλά is ‘even if … yet’. καρτερός is ‘strong’, and θεὰ … μήτηρ ‘a goddess mother’ is Thetis, not named here; γείνατο is the aorist of γείνομαι ‘bore’. ὅ γε is Agamemnon, φέρτερος ‘stronger’, and πλεόνεσσιν ἀνάσσει ‘is lord over more’ (πλεόνεσσιν is the epic dative plural). Nestor’s reasoning is about rank, not about prowess.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδη σὺ δὲ παῦε τεὸν μένος·
sentences.l: And you, Atreus’-son, stop your fury;
sentences.i: And you, son of Atreus, stop your fury;
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative ‘son of Atreus’. παῦε is the aorist imperative of παύω ‘stop’, and τεόν is the epic form of σόν ‘your’. μένος is ‘fury’, as at 207: the same word Athena used to Achilles is now used to Agamemnon.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε
λίσσομ’ Ἀχιλλῆϊ μεθέμεν χόλον, ὃς μέγα πᾶσιν
ἕρκος Ἀχαιοῖσιν πέλεται πολέμοιο κακοῖο.
sentences.l:
but I for my part
beg Achilles to let go his anger, who a great, for all,
fence for the Achaeans is against evil war.”
sentences.i: while I for my part beg Achilles to let go his anger, he who is a great bulwark for all the Achaeans against evil war.”
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε is ‘but I for my part’. λίσσομαι ‘beg’ takes the dative Ἀχιλλῆϊ and the infinitive μεθέμεν (= μεθιέναι) ‘to let go’, with χόλον ‘anger’. ὃς … πέλεται ‘who is’: ἕρκος is a fence or wall of defence (the word used of the teeth in the Odyssey), here a bulwark against πολέμοιο κακοῖο ‘evil war’, for πᾶσιν Ἀχαιοῖσιν ‘all the Achaeans’. The speech ends.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed lord Agamemnon:
sentences.i: In answer lord Agamemnon said to him:
sentences.n: This line is word for word 130, where Agamemnon answered Achilles, and the English is the same. τόν is ‘him’, here Nestor; ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’; προσέφη ‘addressed’. κρείων, ‘lord’ (literally ‘ruling’), is the epithet of Agamemnon here, and the formula opens the next speech.

sentences.t: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε πάντα γέρον κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες·
sentences.l: “Yes indeed, all this, old man, according to what is fitting you have said;
sentences.i: “Yes indeed, old man, all this you have said as is fitting;
sentences.n: ναὶ δή is ‘yes indeed’, a polite agreement before the objection. γέρον is the vocative ‘old man’, ταῦτα … πάντα ‘all this’, and κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘according to what is fitting’, μοῖρα being a due measure. ἔειπες is an epic form of the aorist of εἶπον. The ἀλλά of the next line is where he turns.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅδ’ ἀνὴρ ἐθέλει περὶ πάντων ἔμμεναι ἄλλων,
πάντων μὲν κρατέειν ἐθέλει, πάντεσσι δ’ ἀνάσσειν,
πᾶσι δὲ σημαίνειν, ἅ τιν’ οὐ πείσεσθαι ὀΐω·
sentences.i: But this man wants to be above all others: he wants to rule over everyone, to be lord of everyone, and to give orders to everyone, orders that I think some will not obey;
sentences.n: ὅδ’ ἀνήρ is ‘this man’, pointing at Achilles. ἐθέλει governs four infinitives: ἔμμεναι (= εἶναι) περὶ πάντων ἄλλων ‘to be above all others’, κρατέειν ‘to hold sway’ (with the genitive πάντων), ἀνάσσειν ‘to be lord’ (with the epic dative πάντεσσι) and σημαίνειν ‘to give orders’. ἅ is the relative ‘which’, τιν’ is τινα, and οὐ πείσεσθαι ὀΐω is ‘I think … will not obey’: ὀΐω ‘I think’ takes the future infinitive of πείθομαι.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ μιν αἰχμητὴν ἔθεσαν θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες
τοὔνεκά οἱ προθέουσιν ὀνείδεα μυθήσασθαι;
sentences.l:
and if a spearman him made the gods who are forever,
is it for that reason that reproaches run forward for him to be uttered?”
sentences.i: And if the gods who are forever made him a spearman, is that why insults run forward for him to utter?”
sentences.n: εἰ δέ μιν … ἔθεσαν is ‘and if they made him’. αἰχμητήν is ‘spearman, warrior’, and θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες ‘the gods who are forever’ (αἰέν = ἀεί; ἐόντες is the epic participle of εἰμί), the same phrase as in the Odyssey. τοὔνεκά is ‘for that reason’, οἱ ‘for him’. The syntax of προθέουσιν ὀνείδεα μυθήσασθαι is uncertain; the translation takes ὀνείδεα ‘reproaches’ as the subject of ‘run forward’, with μυθήσασθαι ‘to utter’. The Greek question mark ends the speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑποβλήδην ἠμείβετο δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l: Him then, cutting in, answered heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: Cutting in, heavenly Achilles answered him:
sentences.n: ὑποβλήδην is an adverb formed on ὑποβάλλω ‘throw in under’, ‘by cutting in, taking up the speaker’s words’: Achilles interrupts. τὸν is ‘him’, Agamemnon, ἄρ’ = ἄρα, and ἠμείβετο is ‘answered’. δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is ‘heavenly Achilles’.

sentences.t:
ἦ γάρ κεν δειλός τε καὶ οὐτιδανὸς καλεοίμην
εἰ δὴ σοὶ πᾶν ἔργον ὑπείξομαι ὅττί κεν εἴπῃς·
sentences.l:
“For indeed I should be called both miserable and worthless
if I am to yield to you in every matter, whatever you say;
sentences.i: “I should be called miserable and worthless, if I am to give way to you in every matter, whatever you may say;
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ κεν … καλεοίμην is a potential optative, ‘I would be called’, with κεν. The condition is εἰ … ὑπείξομαι, the future of ὑπείκω ‘yield’, with the dative σοί. δειλός is rendered ‘miserable’, and here ‘cowardly’ is also in play; οὐτιδανός is ‘worthless’, like the οὐτιδανοῖσιν Achilles said Agamemnon rules, at 231. πᾶν ἔργον is ‘in every matter’, and ὅττι κεν εἴπῃς ‘whatever you may say’.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοισιν δὴ ταῦτ’ ἐπιτέλλεο, μὴ γὰρ ἔμοιγε
σήμαιν’·
sentences.l:
Upon others indeed lay these charges, for to me, at least,
do not give orders;
sentences.i: Lay these charges on others, and do not give orders to me;
sentences.n: ἄλλοισιν … ταῦτ’ ἐπιτέλλεο is ‘lay these charges on others’: ἐπιτέλλεο is the present imperative middle of ἐπιτέλλω, the verb of ἔτελλε at 25. μὴ γὰρ ἔμοιγε σήμαιν’ is the prohibition: σήμαινε, the present imperative of σημαίνω ‘give orders’, with ἔμοιγε ‘to me, at least’. The edition prints a stop after σήμαιν’.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἔγωγ’ ἔτι σοὶ πείσεσθαι ὀΐω.
sentences.l: for I, for my part, no longer think I shall obey you.
sentences.i: for I do not think that I shall obey you any longer.
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ ἔγωγ’ ἔτι σοὶ πείσεσθαι ὀΐω is ‘for I for my part no longer think I shall obey you’. ὀΐω ‘I think’ takes the future infinitive πείσεσθαι, and the negative belongs to the thought, ‘I expect not to obey’. ἔτι is ‘any more’, and σοί the dative after πείθομαι.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσι·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: ἄλλο … ἐρέω is ‘I will tell another thing’, with τοι = σοι. The line is word for word one in the Odyssey (apart from the final ν of σῇσιν there), and the English is the same. βάλλεο is the present imperative middle of βάλλω ‘put, throw’, with ἐνὶ φρεσὶ … σῇσι ‘in your own mind’: ἐνί = ἐν, φρεσί the epic dative plural of φρήν ‘mind’, and σῇσι the epic dative plural of σός ‘your own’.

sentences.t:
χερσὶ μὲν οὔ τοι ἔγωγε μαχήσομαι εἵνεκα κούρης
οὔτε σοὶ οὔτέ τῳ ἄλλῳ, ἐπεί μ’ ἀφέλεσθέ γε δόντες·
sentences.l:
With my hands I will not fight, for my part, for the sake of the maiden,
neither with you nor with any other, since you took her away from me, having given her;
sentences.i: I will not fight with my hands for the sake of the maiden, either with you or with anyone else, since you took her away from me after giving her;
sentences.n: χερσὶ μέν … μαχήσομαι is ‘with my hands I will fight’, the future of μάχομαι, set against fighting with words. εἵνεκα κούρης is ‘for the sake of the maiden’, Briseis, not named here. οὔτε σοὶ οὔτέ τῳ ἄλλῳ is ‘neither with you nor with any other’ (τῳ = τινί). ἀφέλεσθε is the aorist middle of ἀφαιρέομαι ‘take away’ and δόντες is ‘having given’; the plural ‘you’ is the army that gave her and Agamemnon who took her.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἄλλων ἅ μοί ἐστι θοῇ παρὰ νηῒ μελαίνῃ
τῶν οὐκ ἄν τι φέροις ἀνελὼν ἀέκοντος ἐμεῖο·
sentences.l:
But of the other things that are mine by my swift black ship,
of those you could not carry off anything, taking it, with me unwilling;
sentences.i: But of the other things I have beside my swift black ship, you could not take and carry off a single one against my will;
sentences.n: τῶν δ’ ἄλλων ἅ μοί ἐστι is ‘but of the other things that are mine’, and the next line repeats τῶν ‘of those’ as the thing taken from. θοῇ … νηῒ μελαίνῃ is ‘swift black ship’, a dative. οὐκ ἄν τι φέροις is a potential optative, ‘you could not carry off anything’, with the aorist participle ἀνελών ‘having taken up’. ἀέκοντος ἐμεῖο is a genitive absolute, ‘with me unwilling’.

sentences.t: εἰ δ’ ἄγε μὴν πείρησαι ἵνα γνώωσι καὶ οἵδε·
sentences.l: But come now, indeed, make trial, so that they may know, these also;
sentences.i: But come, try it, so that these men too may know it;
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἄγε μήν is an exhortation, ‘but come now’; εἰ here is part of the idiom, not ‘if’. πείρησαι is the aorist imperative of πειράομαι ‘try, make trial’. ἵνα γνώωσι is ‘so that they may know’ (an epic aorist subjunctive), and καὶ οἵδε ‘these also’ points at the Achaeans standing in the assembly.

sentences.t: αἶψά τοι αἷμα κελαινὸν ἐρωήσει περὶ δουρί.
sentences.l: quickly your dark blood will gush around the spear.”
sentences.i: quickly your dark blood will gush about my spear.”
sentences.n: αἶψα is ‘quickly’, and τοι = σοι ‘your’, a dative of interest. ἐρωήσει is the future of ἐρωέω ‘rush, gush’, and αἷμα κελαινόν ‘dark blood’. περὶ δουρί is ‘around the spear’, which is Achilles’ own. He ends with a plain threat, and the speech ends.

sentences.t:
ὣς τώ γ’ ἀντιβίοισι μαχεσσαμένω ἐπέεσσιν
ἀνστήτην, λῦσαν δ’ ἀγορὴν παρὰ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l:
So the two of them, having fought with words of opposition,
stood up, and broke up the assembly by the ships of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: So the two of them, after fighting with opposing words, stood up and broke up the assembly by the ships of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: τώ γε is the dual ‘those two’, with the dual participle μαχεσσαμένω ‘having fought’ (epic doubled σ) and the dual verb ἀνστήτην ‘they stood up’; λῦσαν is the plural aorist ‘they broke up’ (unaugmented). ἀντιβίοισι ἐπέεσσιν is ‘with opposing words’, ἀντίβιος meaning ‘face to face, hostile’. ἀγορήν is the assembly, held παρὰ νηυσίν ‘by the ships’, νηυσίν being the epic dative plural.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης μὲν ἐπὶ κλισίας καὶ νῆας ἐΐσας
ἤϊε σύν τε Μενοιτιάδῃ καὶ οἷς ἑτάροισιν·
sentences.l:
Peleus’-son to the huts and the well-balanced ships
went, with the son of Menoetius and his own companions;
sentences.i: The son of Peleus went to the huts and the well-balanced ships, with the son of Menoetius and his own companions;
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης μέν … Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ (next line) sets the two kings side by side. κλισίας are ‘huts’, and νῆας ἐΐσας ‘well-balanced ships’: the sense of ἐΐσας, ‘equal, balanced’, is not certain when said of a ship. ἤϊε is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘went’. Μενοιτιάδῃ, ‘son of Menoetius’, is Patroclus; οἷς ἑτάροισιν is ‘his own companions’, οἷς being the possessive, not the relative.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ἄρα νῆα θοὴν ἅλα δὲ προέρυσσεν,
ἐν δ’ ἐρέτας ἔκρινεν ἐείκοσιν, ἐς δ’ ἑκατόμβην
βῆσε θεῷ, ἀνὰ δὲ Χρυσηΐδα καλλιπάρῃον
εἷσεν ἄγων·
sentences.l:
And Atreus’-son a swift ship to the salt-sea drew forth,
and in oarsmen picked, twenty, and on board a hecatomb
made go, for the god, and up Chryseis, fair-cheeked,
set, leading her;
sentences.i: The son of Atreus launched a swift ship into the salt sea, picked out twenty oarsmen for her, put a hecatomb on board for the god, and led Chryseis, fair-cheeked, up and seated her;
sentences.n: ἅλα δέ has the suffix -δε of direction, ‘to the sea’, and προέρυσσεν is the aorist (with the epic doubled σ) of προερύω ‘draw forth’. ἐν δ’ ἐρέτας ἔκρινεν is ‘and he picked oarsmen in’, ἐν standing as an adverb. ἐς … βῆσε is the causative aorist of βαίνω, ‘made go on board’; ἑκατόμβην … θεῷ is a hecatomb for the god. ἀνὰ … εἷσεν is a tmesis, ‘set up’, the aorist of ἵζω in its causative use, and ἄγων ‘leading’.

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ ἀρχὸς ἔβη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l: and in as leader went many-wiled Odysseus.
sentences.i: and Odysseus of many wiles went on board as commander.
sentences.n: ἐν … ἔβη is ‘went in’, i.e. on board, with ἀρχός ‘leader, commander’ in apposition to the subject. πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς is ‘many-wiled Odysseus’, the stock epithet of Odysseus: μῆτις is cunning intelligence.
